hints: Notice the incoming straight parallel wavefronts on the left and that the gap in the barrier is described as small, about the size of the wavelength.
Recall that diffraction is strongest when gap width is similar to $\lambda$, causing the gap to act like a new point source of circular waves.
Compare the curvature after the gap: look for smooth semicircular wavefronts spreading widely with the same spacing as the incoming waves.
walkthrough: Identify the set-up: straight plane water wavefronts travel to the right toward a barrier with a small central gap.
State the rule: diffraction spreads waves through a gap, and the effect is maximum when gap width is of order $\lambda$. The wavelength and speed do not change on passing through.
The gap then acts approximately as a point source, so the transmitted wavefronts become circular arcs centred on the gap and spread into the shadow region behind the barrier.
Check spacing: the distance between successive arcs after the gap must equal the distance between the incoming straight lines, because $\lambda$ is unchanged.
Only diagram A shows wide, smooth, concentric semicircular arcs spreading well beyond the gap width with unchanged spacing. This is option A.

options.A: Shows strong diffraction with plane waves becoming near-circular wavefronts centred on the small gap, with wavelength unchanged.
options.B: Shows only slight curvature near the centre and a detached wavefront, not the wide circular spreading expected when gap width is similar to wavelength.
options.C: Shows distorted wavy lines rather than smooth circular diffracted wavefronts spreading from the gap.
options.D: Shows wavefronts that remain almost straight and parallel, which is transmission with little diffraction, not correct for a small gap.
